akikiie.name: Akikiie
akikiie.html:
Aki — Silveh on Discord — built the house the Dusk era lived in: the first message in the entire officer-chat archive is him, in April 2020, setting up the Ninjas server with its gated roles and class channels. He was a Ninjas officer, a warrior with fifty-eight raid nights, and a steady tactical voice through the AQ progression — the man explaining Huhuran nature-resistance splits and Twin Emperor gear swaps in paragraphs while others argued in fragments.

His guild life ended on a single pull. On 17 September 2020 he pulled at the Ahn'Qiraj entrance with nobody ready, the world buffs died, Ulfhild rage-quit, and three days of officer warfare followed. Aki owned it completely — "I'll happily apologise and take the blame for it. It's not my intent to hide from it" — and then asked the question underneath the whole affair: whether he actually enjoyed a game where a single wipe could ruin forty people's evening. He decided he didn't, and left within the week. His raid log ends on the night of the pull; the archive remembers him as both the architect of the guild's home and the first casualty of its seriousness.

suspected alts — co-absence analysis.name: Suspected alts — co-absence analysis
suspected alts — co-absence analysis.html:
Generated 2026-07-30 from canonical Warcraft Logs rosters. Method (Anders's idea): for each low-session character that joined two or more months into the archive, find high-attendance mains who were active in the same window and lineages but absent from essentially every raid the candidate alt attended (at most one shared session, which allows a mid-raid character swap — Artimis/Lege share three sessions that way). The score is how improbable the main's absences are given their normal attendance rate; higher is more suspicious.

None of these are in `alts.json` yet — promote a pair only after confirmation (a Discord statement, a workbook comment, or Anders/participant memory). Validated confirmed pairs (Rocka→Rockafella, Yukikitsune→Glorya) show the same signature this analysis looks for.

## Strong — name similarity plus co-absence

All four confirmed by Anders 2026-07-30 and promoted to `alts.json`: Devouboi→Devou, Hiltsey→Hilts, Steewie→Steewiee, Tsiko→Tsakimo.

## Medium — co-absence only, plausible

| Suspected alt | Candidate main | Signal | |---|---|---| | Holyhans (Paladin, 11n, Jun–Sep) | Dolleboy (Druid) | 0 shared at 0.68; Dolleboy also pairs with Powerhealer (Priest, 6n) at 0.73 — one main, possibly two alts | | Wetfarter (Hunter, 11n, Jun–Sep) | Amberlynreid (Rogue) | 0 shared at 0.68 | | Maevis (Mage, 12n, Jun–Oct) | Rangah (Hunter) | 0 shared at 0.63 | | Nonstickpan (Rogue, 10n, Jun–Oct) | Saltyhead (Rogue) | 0 shared at 0.68; same class weakens it | | Melic (Hunter, 16n, Apr–Sep) | Mysor (Rogue) | 1 shared at 0.59 | | Gallithian (Mage, 11n, May–Aug) | Exhopresso (Warrior) | 0 shared at 0.58 | | Darkranger (Hunter, 5n, May–Jun) | Divinestorm (Mage) | 0 shared at 0.56; small sample — but ask Divinestorm, it would be a fun detail |

## Weak or likely explained

- Namelessqt, Subroza, and Aggeeinn all pair with Crok in Oct–Dec windows — more likely Crok simply attended less that autumn than that he ran three alts; treat as noise unless confirmed. - Filippoberio pairs with Ragie statistically, but the Dusk officer chat treats Filippo as his own person ("Deltron and Filippo were benched") — rejected. - Mdsthesecond (Priest, 5n) — the name says "the second [character]" of someone; statistics point weakly at Priestå or Spaxi. The name alone makes it worth asking about. - Divinehealer (Priest, 8n, Oct–Feb) pairs with Glorya/Selephie at low confidence; Glorya's confirmed alt is the rogue Yukikitsune, so a second priest alt is unlikely. - Mikai (Rogue, 5n) pairs weakly with Amberlynreid; note the unresolved Mika/Mikadro/Mikasalord name cluster from the loot workbook.

## How to confirm

Ask in the Dusk Discord or during participant interviews; check the workbook comment column for the main's name on the alt's loot rows; or search the officer chat for the alt's name. On confirmation, add to `alts.json` and note the evidence in `alts-evidence.md`.

## Candidates — named but unconfirmed

- Arcanefarts (Mage, 34 sessions): Jón Snjór, 2020-09-10: "we could maybe ask arcanefarts since its his alt and he was gonna move to wednesday group"; Banamahs adds the owner is "on call" certain weeks. The owner is an unnamed mage-team member in a bench discussion (Kolfinna? Filippo?). Needs one more source. - Neptun (Mage, 33 workbook rows, ZG attendance leader): Anders's hypothesis — Ragie's second account or Henriette (Ragie's girlfriend). Ask Ragie. - Rocka (6 workbook rows): shorthand for Rockafella or a separate alt; "Samie and Rocka rolled" comments treat it as a person. Unresolved. - Deepdive: "Deepdive won roll" comment on a Catstrangler row 2020-06-14; name appears nowhere else. Unresolved.

## Known alts without recovered names

Drekka has a priest; Òllz a warlock; Ferrua a priest; Powerranger a paladin (all from Dusk officer chat, character names never stated).

antzi.name: Antzi
antzi.html:
Antzi ran the rogues — before the merger in Ninjas, after it in Dusk — and brought to the officer chat a philosophy he repeated until everyone could recite it: focus is respect. He didn't care if you came unbuffed; he cared if you wasted thirty-nine other people's evening. "I play this game for the community," he wrote in one of the autumn's better manifestos, and meant it literally — his rogues never once made loot drama, a record he defended with visible pride.

His temper was the cost of the conviction. The September crises pulled him into shouting matches with Divinestorm ("no brain pull"), with Rockafella ("stick to ur lock"), and into the Band of Accuria blowup where he heard himself called stupid and demanded it never happen again. But the record consistently shows the anger pointing somewhere real: at carelessness, at gift-loot logic, at anything that treated the raid's time as free. When he admitted he'd talked his rogues out of quitting "with arguments I don't even believe," it was the most honest sentence of the whole autumn.

artimis.name: Artimis
artimis.html:
Artimis joined Dejvid's young guild in the autumn of 2019 and was soon running it in practice — formally from February 2020, when Dejvid handed over the reins. He ran it the way he ran everything: with spreadsheets. The attendance workbook, the loot log (started 2020-03-29 with a plea that class leaders post every drop), the raider-rank system with its promise that showing up mattered — all of it was his architecture, and most of it outlived his tenure. As a hunter he chased the Rhok'delar quest line alongside his recruits; as an alchemist he ran a one-man consumables service, mailing flasks to tanks and crafting anything anyone needed. His priest alt Lege healed whenever the roster came up short.

He gave the guild away twice. In early 2020 he offered the leadership to Kodf, who declined; in August 2020, minutes after a Nefarian kill, he told the raid that Divinestorm would be the new Guild Master and thanked everyone for their trust — handing over the guild mid-raid, in the same breath as a boss kill. He stayed on as the institutional memory: teaching the spreadsheets, mediating disputes, and writing the rules other people argued about.

December 2020 made him the story's protagonist against his will. When the Ascension merge cut the roster to twenty and the promises of the raider-rank system stopped being honoured, Artimis — himself benched from every single Four Horsemen attempt — wrote a five-point proposal demanding raiders before members, whole-lockout spots, and collective bench decisions, and asked members to strike. The strike never happened; the guild dissolved into Ascension two days later. He kept raiding into 2021, kept the records, and years later those records became this site.

banamahs.name: Banamahs
banamahs.html:
Banamahs led the Thursday mages and thought about guilds the way an economist thinks about fisheries: the resource is your members' time and goodwill, and every scuffed raid overfishes it. "Longevity is the key to this game," he wrote in September, "but if you burn resources too quickly, people quit." He said it about continuation raids, about split-run chaos, about consumable costs — and the autumn kept proving him right.

He was the calm half of the Ninjas bloc: building loot-overview spreadsheets other class leaders copied, absorbing a mage exodus (three top-geared mages gone in a week) with recruitment plans instead of drama, and cutting through the era's worst arguments with lines like "this wasn't a case of afk players — we were not ready to pull." His tribute to Ulfhild doubles as his own epitaph for the era: if everyone pumped that hard, the raid would take forty-five minutes.

boxya.name: Boxya
boxya.html: Boxya's guild career is a two-act comedy of timing. Recruited by Luivi as a friend of Wandolina, he signed up for a September raid, never showed, and left the guild the next day. Yet by December he was back and suddenly indispensable: picked as one of Dusk's two protected tanks in the Ascension merge — and then he left again, days later, forcing Ragie into the spot. Two departures, both at the worst possible moment; the tank crisis that drove the December merge has his fingerprints on it.

celed.name: Celed
celed.html: Celed was a rogue from the Ninjas line who held the class-leader seat as a stand-in when Antzi's work schedule bit, and gave it back with the most graceful resignation in the record: "Antzi wants to replace me! We talked about it so much and this is our decision... he knows so much about the game. I'll help going forward." No drama, no politics, a 72-raid resume, and a healer-parse joke at his expense that followed him around one autumn week ("95 parse is worthy of some loot, actually"). The guild ran on its arguers; it also ran on people like Celed, who mostly just showed up and played well.

crok.name: Crok
crok.html: Crok was a mage with 164 raids in the logs — one of the most-attended players in the whole archive — and the pragmatist in the officer chat. When rosters ran short he suggested filling with pugs and recruiting the good ones ("worked in the past"); when December's crisis meetings ran hot he stayed practical. His DM thread with Anders spans the guild's whole life, from a February 2020 recruit conversation to three days after the Kel'Thuzad kill. He farmed venom sacks on the night crew, carried the Ring of Spiritual Fervor out of the 12-wipe Horsemen night, and made the jump to Ascension with the rest.

deliz.name: Deliz
deliz.html:
Deliz was a healer, one of the guild's Norwegian core, and the story's first fairness casualty. In February 2020 — a year before anyone had heard of Ascension — he quit WoW over how healers were treated: excluded from best-in-slot rolls while the damage dealers geared, with a disputed Ragnaros neck as the concrete grievance. His exit put a question on the table that the guild never fully answered, and that returned in every later crisis: what does the raid owe the people who keep it alive but never top a meter?

His friendship with Anders long outlasted his raiding. The messages run from 2019 to 2025 — game recommendations, life updates, and the occasional piece of guild news from the outside, including the December 2020 note that Chris had deleted the old WoW Classic Discord. In the story of Sleep he is the early warning: the guild's kindest era already contained the argument that would end it.

devou.name: Devou
devou.html: Devou was Ascension's warrior officer and the other half of the December negotiation. From the Dusk side of the record he appears as a fair counterpart: the one who offered his own raid spot to a benched Dusk hunter on the first joint night ("thank Devou," Divinestorm insisted, "for understanding how much we wanted a 3rd hunter spot"), and the firm no when a fourth hunter spot was floated. Ascension wanted to stay Ascension and absorb Dusk; he said so openly from day one, which is more than most mergers get. The Ascension side of this story — the KT week, the January era — is still waiting for his version.

divinestorm.name: Divinestorm
divinestorm.html:
Divinestorm arrived as a mage in February 2020 and ended the year as the guild's center of gravity. His rise ran through every institution the guild had: mage class leader by late April, channel-architect and document-keeper after the Dusk merger, author of the loot doctrine — effort measured in attendance, world buffs, consumables and consistency, with the council keeping the final word — and ultimately guild master. The officer chat shows him everywhere: running the idol economy item by item, defending benched players one day ("we solved problems for the top raiders, but we haven't solved it for those we bench") and defending hard calls the next ("I have no problem making hard calls if needed").

He was also the guild's shock absorber. When September 2020 delivered a crisis a week — a ninja pull, a rage-quit, an officer resigning in the chat, a kick war that briefly cost the guild its own tank leader — Divinestorm mediated all of them, often from work trips, and wrote the member-facing statements afterwards. And when Naxxramas exposed the tank roster in December, it was Divinestorm who concluded overnight that the guild could not continue alone, opened talks with Ascension's officers, and within eight days led Dusk's mass migration — planning it, fittingly, as everyone hearthed into the raid. The 15/15 Kel'Thuzad kill four days later happened under his leadership.

His personality is all over the record: the man who bought poison sacs by the hundred and tracked idol distribution person by person; who defended a benched no-name because "the guy worked really hard farming sacs for us"; who called himself "the mage who didn't understand hunter loot" while arbitrating a hunter loot fight. He absorbed abuse that would have broken pettier leaders — sworn at in officer chat, told to his face the leadership was running the guild into the ground — and answered with the same maddening evenness that made people trust him with the December decisions.

History's verdict on those decisions is the story's hardest question. The pivot to Ascension saved the raid — 15/15 in fourteen days proves it — and it cost the guild its identity and its most loyal bench. Both things are true, and Divinestorm, who took the blame for a botched benching in the same breath as he claimed the authority to bench anyone, seems to have understood that better than anyone at the time.

edomedo.name: Edomedo
edomedo.html: Edomedo was the tank-in-waiting whose exit changed everything. Groomed through November as the contingency ("we have a potential tank lined up"), he preferred tanking to DPS and said so. On the night of December 7th 2020 he told Divinestorm he was quitting the game — and that single conversation set off the chain reaction: no tanks for Four Horsemen, the overnight partnership with Ascension, the twenty-spot cut, and the end of Dusk nine days later. Few players this quiet ever moved a story this much.

ferrua.name: Ferrua
ferrua.html:
Ferrua was a warlock from the Ninjas side with a talent for being the adult in the room. He is the officer whose loot judgment aged best — "turns out Ferrua was right not to give Mika the Rejuv Gem," Luivi conceded months later — and the one who ended up running healer loot on zero notice the day Orish quit ("Does this mean I decide healer loot today?" — "You'll have to"). He did it well enough that nobody complained, which in this guild counts as a standing ovation.

His interventions were short and usually decisive: on rage-quitting ("imagine if ten people rage quit — we have no raid"), on second chances, on defending Divinestorm when the criticism turned personal. He argued for diversity in raid comps on principle — "imagine if we only had warriors and paladins, that would suck" — and kept a dry banter ledger with Dan about vendorstrike luck. One of the quiet load-bearers.

fizzi.name: Fizzi
fizzi.html:
Fizzi was a warrior who treated raid rosters like an engineering problem. By late 2020 he was the Dusk officer doing the unglamorous math: how many hunter spots a merged raid could carry, which classes were oversubscribed, who could tank Four Horsemen if Boxya disappeared again (he kept Edomedo warm as the contingency). When the December merge happened, he was one of the two tanks Dusk protected in the first brutal cut — and he'd earned it, having tanked C'Thun with Glory just weeks earlier.

His philosophy was stated plainly in the December debates: comp plus parse — with limited spots you bring the players who perform, and "bench decisions… I have no problem making hard calls if needed." But the same person argued for alt-and-member loot parity in November, defended benched players' access to gear, and did the tedious work of maintaining signup tabs and week-three spreadsheets that fairness actually runs on.

He was in the first Four Horsemen kill and the Kel'Thuzad clear, and carried on into Ascension's farm era — one of the people whose December choices the story judges gently, because the archive shows how much thought went into them.

glory.name: Glory
glory.html:
Glory joined in mid-February 2020, recruited almost by accident — Anders initially mistook him for someone else and had already mailed him a cloak. He became one of the guild's fixtures: a protection warrior with over 120 raids and 96% attendance, a blacksmith who could forge five of the six Radiant pieces for the Naxxramas frost-resistance push, and by December 2020 the owner of a completed Thunderfury — one of the guild's few.

His story is the loyalist's tragedy. As early as March 2020 he was asking for nothing more than a fair system, arguing that effort at the bottom of the meters deserved the same respect as parses at the top. He tanked C'Thun for Dusk as late as November. But when the December merge with Ascension cut the roster to twenty spots, Glory never got a single Four Horsemen pull — not one of the twelve wipes, not the kill. On the afternoon of the first kill he was told he had a spot that evening; the raid one-shot the fight without him while he listened to the strategy briefing from the bench. Two days later, on the same evening the guild mass-migrated into Ascension, he left — "better to go during the change" — saying the guild had been his home and that even a place every other week would have kept him. Within a week he was tanking Four Horsemen for another guild. Invited back after the 15/15 clear, he decided he could not abandon the people who had given him a spot. His last word in the archive, from 2022: not playing WoW any more, for now.

The archive can now date every beat of that December. He tanked C'Thun for Dusk on November 12th. He was in none of the twelve Four Horsemen wipes on December 13th. At 14:21 on the 14th he told Anders the guild master had given him a spot that evening; at 19:42 the Horsemen died on the night's first pull with forty other names in the log. The officers' private verdict that same day — a year and a half of trial, not improved, not good enough — was never said to his face; Anders, asked directly who had blocked him, refused to name names, and the archive kept the secret for five years.

What makes Glory's story more than a grievance is how completely the record vindicates his effort. He was second only to a handful in raids attended. He funded and forged his own gear. He respecced deep Protection the afternoon of a fight he never got to tank, and when his new guild put him in front of the Four Horsemen the following week, he tanked them competently. The question his story asks — whether a guild owes loyalty to the loyal — was the same one Anders's strike letter asked, written on the same day, and neither man got an answer.

glorya.name: Glorya
glorya.html:
Glorya — Knut, one of the guild's Norwegians — was a priest healer whose name caused two years of clerical confusion with the warrior Glory, a coincidence the archive has to untangle on nearly every page. The two could hardly have had more different Decembers: while Glory watched the Four Horsemen progression from the bench, Glorya healed it — he is in the roster of the first kill on December 14th and stayed for the full Kel'Thuzad clear.

He was part of the healer core that made the merge attractive to Ascension in the first place — Dusk's healing was its export product — and the kind of steady presence who shows up in the logs far more often than in the drama. When raids ran late or short-handed, Glorya arriving "potentially a little bit late" with Pnats was a recurring line in the healer logistics. His tribute video sits on Supplier's 2021 "Dusk list," between Shakey's and Carmelia's.

hedara.name: Hedara
hedara.html: Hedara was Ascension's druid officer, the second name Divinestorm gave Dusk when the December partnership formed. The archive holds less of him than his role deserves: a healer in the first Four Horsemen kill and the Kel'Thuzad clear, a short friendly DM with Anders about whether they'd met before ("You're from Norway, right? Your voice is familiar"), and a place in every joint-raid roster through the clear. Like Devou, he is a door this story hasn't opened yet — the Ascension officer chat from December would answer questions this archive can only pose.

henne.name: Henne
henne.html:
Henne — Linda — came over from the Ninjas side and became one of the voices that bridged the two cultures. Her guild life ended as collateral damage in the strangest day of the Dusk era: on September 30th 2020, when Jón Snjór was kicked without warning, he used his alt's rank to kick Henne in retaliation before anyone could react. The protest gquits that followed nearly took the guild apart, and Anders's first message to her that afternoon — let's find out what happened and find a fair solution — opens one of the archive's DM threads.

She was restored along with everyone else once Divinestorm untangled the mess, and the incident forced the reform that outlived it: kick rights were restricted, and "if you don't have time to explain, you should not have time to kick people" became guild doctrine. Few players did less to deserve their place in the drama, which is precisely why her name is on the reform.

jellopy.name: Jellopy
jellopy.html: Jellopy was the guild's first rogue class leader, running the class in the early BWL era with a five-slot raider roster he picked himself. In February 2020 real life pulled him away — "not sure when or if he is coming back," Anders told Kodf while offering him the permanent seat — and his quiet exit created the succession that gave the rogues their golden age. He is the archive's reminder that most guild history isn't drama: sometimes the important people just log off.

kodf.name: Kodf
kodf.html:
Kodf ran the rogues, and for a while he quietly ran much of the guild. Promoted to permanent rogue class leader in February 2020 when Jellopy drifted away, he built the loot system his class became famous for — fair enough that months after he left, officers were still wishing someone could "do Kodf's system." His officer-chat exchanges with Artimis in March 2020 are the guild's constitutional debates: hunters versus rogues on weapon priority, how much a member who shows up is owed, whether kindness or performance should decide the marginal raid spot.

He was also the road not taken. When Artimis looked for a successor, Kodf was the first offer — take over Sleep — and he declined, choosing in September 2020 to follow his own path into the guild Conviction. He left the way he did everything: tidily, with explanations, and he kept helping his old guildmates afterwards.

His fingerprints stayed on the guild long after his name left the roster: the rogue loot queues, the expectation that a class leader actually leads, and a small mystery he'd be amused by — the officers spent the autumn debating "another Kodf" and never quite found one.

kugel.name: Kugel
kugel.html:
Kugel was the original main tank — the warrior the guild built its first raids around, and an early recipient of a Binding of the Windseeker back when handing a legendary component to your main tank seemed obviously right. Then, in January 2020, he simply stopped logging in. Twenty-three days of silence later the officers were asking around ("if he misses next BWL i think we should demote him"), by February the main-tank vacancy was official, and in March he was quietly removed from the roster after two months offline.

His disappearance shaped the guild twice over. It handed the tank mantle to Ragie and opened the gearing question that Glory, Zhena, and later Jón Snjór would each live through in turn. And the Binding that left with him became guild doctrine: from then on, legendary priority was tied to reliability and long-term commitment — a rule written, like most guild rules, in response to a specific disappointment. Nobody in the archive ever says where he went.

luivi.name: Luivi
luivi.html:
Luivi was the druid class leader whose one decision reshaped the whole story: in July 2020, Sleep offered him the guild-master seat. He turned it down — no time for it — and instead asked his contacts in Ninjas whether they'd consider merging. That conversation became Dusk. It's hard to name a more consequential "no" in the guild's history.

As a leader he ran the druids with visible pride ("Druids, the most civilized Class") and a warm, blunt style that survived translation from his native language into rapid-fire officer-chat English. He was the patient center of the Nayla saga — voting for a last warning while admitting the man exhausted him — and the one who kept perspective when officer arguments overheated: no one was dying, the content was getting cleared, chill out a bit.

He raided everywhere: main raids on Luivi, fill-ins on his alt Vikka, off-tanking in cat spec when asked, venom-sack farm runs until he literally fell asleep at the keyboard mid-session (the officers renamed the voice channel "Sleepy Luivi" and tiptoed out). He became a Dusk officer in September, made the jump to Ascension in December, and stayed one of the last active voices in the old officer channel deep into 2021.

missdotty.name: Missdotty
missdotty.html:
Missdotty — Dotty, or Decretum on Discord — was a warlock, the Thursday team's off-boss tank when a fight demanded one, and the officer chat's investigator-in-chief. When idols went missing from the guild bank pipeline, Dotty traced them mailbox by mailbox ("the investigator!"); when arguments ran to 150 messages, Dotty arrived late, sighed "99% shit, 1% information, as usual," and set up a poll. The Among Us jokes wrote themselves, and Dotty leaned in.

The record also holds one running comedy of mistaken identity: half the guild spent months assuming Missdotty was a woman, a discovery that cost Pnats a genuine crisis ("She's not?" — "I can be, if you want"). Beyond the jokes sat a reliable officer: hardline in the Nayla debate, generous in the Tear queue (giving up a claim so Potema could have it), and the one who kept Discord's machinery — polls, roles, tags — actually working.

nayla.name: Nayla
nayla.html:
Nayla was a feral druid and off-tank whose two years in the guild produced more officer-chat discussion than almost anyone else's. He was generous with his time — always available, always signed — and famously difficult to pin down: conversations relayed through him had a way of arriving changed, to the point where officers joked they needed screenshots.

His defining month was the autumn of 2020. An apparent ninja pull in AQ20 turned out, on investigation, to be a misunderstanding — he had been teleported onto the boss while trying to hearth out — but it landed on top of older friction, and the officers split between removal and mercy. The verdict, after a night of debate that ranged from "his behavior is toxic" to "loyalty you can't buy": one final chance, framed as a fresh start for the new guild. He lost his tank spot soon after, flirted with rerolling rogue, and was still being proposed for raider rank as late as October. On 25 November he left in a burst of drama, messaging guild members that their leader had committed a "last desperate act of evilness" — the details of which the archive still doesn't record. By December he had found a new guild and a new audience on the realm Discord. His story is the guild's hardest governance question in miniature: what do you owe the member who gives you everything and costs you almost as much?

The record is unusually rich on how he was experienced by others: the class leader who defended him ("a soul whose intentions are good") in the same message as admitting he was exhausting; the officers who communicated with him only in pairs so there would be a witness; the running joke that no two people ever heard the same version of a conversation with him. When he told one officer he had "lost his tanking spot," the officer who supposedly took it away had no idea what he was talking about — a small scene that explains his whole file.

And yet the guild kept almost keeping him. He survived a removal announcement, earned back a bench slot, and was seriously proposed for raider rank six weeks before the end. Whatever the "last desperate act of evilness" was that he announced on his way out, within two weeks he was raiding elsewhere and loudly himself on the realm Discord — proof, in its way, that there was never anything wrong with his will to play.

nereb.name: Nereb
nereb.html: Nereb was the third hunter in the rotation that defined December — the agreement by which he, Artimis and Zados took turns sitting out when the merged raid allowed the class only a few spots. He'd been there from the early days, one of the hunters chasing Rhok'delar leaves in the winter of 2019-2020, and he was in the first Four Horsemen kill on the night both his rotation partners watched from outside. In the debates about hunter spots he was one of the three names even the hardliners agreed had to be protected: "Artimis is a special case, so is Zados and Nereb."

orish.name: Orish
orish.html:
Orish — Dan on Discord — was the Thursday raid's healing brain and the most quotable internal critic the guild ever had. He came over with Ninjas, built the healer loot plans item by item, leveled three warlocks just to run summons for other people's world buffs, and defended his turf in prose that still crackles: anyone trying to snake healing loot without knowing the role would "be dealing with me, one to one."

He fought with almost everyone worth fighting with — the priest channel, the Sunday-raid planners, and above all Divinestorm, in a September feud that produced the officer chat's most profane sentence and its sharpest critiques. The thing about Orish's criticism was that it was mostly right: the split-run chaos he attacked was real, the communication gaps were real, and the members left in the dark were real. On 24 September 2020, undermined once too often on healer decisions, he quit live in the channel — "Leadership's going to run this guild into the ground, I'm out before it gets much worse" — and took his alts with him. The officers restructured their entire chat within the hour. It was, in its way, his last accepted proposal.

pawsz.name: Pawsz
pawsz.html:
Pawsz was a druid, a Ninjas officer, and the closest thing the officer chat had to a house intellectual — the one running the numbers on venom sac consumption per Viscidus attempt, proposing member polls with properly phrased questions, and arguing for radical transparency when everyone else wanted PR ("we can just let people read the officer chat. I don't care one bit how it looks"). His one-liners carried more policy than most meetings: "we are not the UN"; "Stoneshield is not something one pops for personal parsing."

He was also the merger's honest observer. It was Pawsz who noted the irony that the supposedly weaker Sleep brought the stricter rules, and Pawsz who refused to let September's departures become a Ninjas-versus- Sleep story: "We are not sat here pointing at Nayla either — why make this about Ninjas and Sleep again?" When the factions finally dissolved into Ascension in December, he was still there, still auditing the decision-making, still allergic to nonsense.

pnats.name: Pnats
pnats.html:
Pnats was a resto druid, Ragie's brother, and the officer chat's conscience. With 144 raids behind him he had the standing to say uncomfortable things, and he used it: when Artimis was benched in December, it was Pnats who opened the debate — the value the man had brought to Sleep and Dusk deserved better — and when the officers needed someone to state the hard truth about Glory, he did that too, in words that were kinder in intent than on the page.

He was the connective tissue of three guilds. He healed Sleep's raids from 2019, became a Dusk officer at the September 2020 meeting, worried constantly about healer recruitment ("we lost so many healers"), and kept the loot log honest. He also supplied the archive's comic relief — the discovery that Missdotty was not, in fact, a woman, cost him a genuine crisis of confidence — and its most quoted line: on the day Dusk dissolved, he pinged the officers with "BYE DUSK?" and then, at midnight, wrote the era's epitaph: "its been good Sleep > Dusk > Ascension, we've done it all."

He raided on through Ascension's Naxxramas farm into 2021, logged onto his brother's warrior when the roster needed it, and stayed the person people forwarded screenshots to when something dramatic happened — which, in this guild, was often.

ragie.name: Ragie
ragie.html:
Ragie — Jack on Discord, Pnats's brother — was the guild's tank spine across every era. He inherited the main-tank mantle when Kugel vanished in early 2020, and from then on the records rarely show a serious raid without him: Dark Iron gear crafted specifically so the guild could get past Firemaw, the tank-loot priority debates of spring 2020 (in which Glory saw him as the favoured rival), and by the Dusk era the formal role of tank leader, raid-leading Sunday runs alongside Jón Snjór.

He is also half of the guild's longest-running loot argument. The question of what a main tank was owed — first claim on mitigation gear, crafting materials, a Thunderfury — put him repeatedly opposite Glory, whose grievances about "Ragie gets anything he wants" date to March 2020. The archive is fairer to both men than they were to each other: Ragie's gearing was policy, argued openly in officer channels, and the binding runs that eventually completed Thunderfuries were organised for him and others by name.

He was in the first Four Horsemen kill and the 15/15, made the move to Ascension with everyone on the day of the migration — Pnats pinged him to take one last look at the dying Dusk channel — and kept tanking into 2022 in the guild's afterlife.

randyfist.name: Randyfist
randyfist.html:
Randyfist — Randy, or Trenfentson on Discord — is one of the archive's quiet constants: a paladin who held the healing-officer role back in early Sleep, reappeared through every era, and by late Dusk was the officer chat's resident hawk. When the December merge talks began, his counsel was piracy: "poach the benched Ascension raiders, cancel the merge, Ascension implodes, we get half their shit — just like a good ol' divorce." Nobody took the advice. Everybody quoted it.

He recruited paladins when nobody else would ("Recruit yourself, Randy," Divinestorm shot back), tanked the Four Horsemen first kill, and asked the question that ended Dusk — "When we leaving and merging?" — then answered it himself within twenty minutes: "Fuck it, get it over and done with. Gonna do it there now; it's good to have some officers already in there before the migration." His OCD, he explained, flared at unresolved things.

rockafella.name: Rockafella
rockafella.html:
Rockafella was a warlock and one of the guild's institutionalists — the voice that said the quiet part about Dusk's governance out loud: "Class leaders think they are officers. If the class leaders could shut their mouths and run their class and let the officers manage the guild, we wouldn't have this shit." Within the hour, the officers split the chat in two. Few messages in the archive changed more structure faster.

He shows up wherever the record needs a witness with standing: talking Nayla's case through with Divinestorm and establishing that the infamous AQ20 "ninja pull" was a hearthstone misunderstanding; holding the line in the Band of Accuria fight ("we're trying to move away from a culture where the one who shouts loudest is right"); and tanking in the first Four Horsemen kill. He wanted a guild run by its officers, and mostly, after September, he got one.

shakeyhealer.name: Shakeyhealer
shakeyhealer.html: Shakey was a priest, an officer, and one of the guild's steady hands — the kind of presence who appears in every era's records without ever being the problem. In the Glory affair he was one of the two named supporters ("Zados and Shakey has always been for you," Anders told Glory on the night he quit), and his healing anchored the December raids: he is in the first Four Horsemen kill roster and stayed through the clear. His DM thread with Anders is one of the largest in the archive — 562 messages of guild logistics across the whole of 2020 — and one of the least dramatic, which is its own kind of biography.

snjór.name: Snjór
snjór.html:
Jón Snjór — Snjór in the raid, Fantur on his warrior alt — came from Iceland with the Ninjas, held their raid leadership, and owned the Dusk Discord server itself. His tank career is the guild's clearest document of what off-tanking actually cost in Classic: asked to hold Twin Emperors on a second-string gear set, he laid out the math — five thousand gold of Edgemaster's, double consumables, five-point-nine thousand health against five-thousand-damage strikes — and the year's most quietly devastating line: "I've been saying this for weeks, and the answer was like, yeah, we can get someone else to do it."

He led Sunday raids, recruited half the server's strays, took responsibility for things that weren't his fault ("I told them to direct their anger at me"), and became the center of the era's worst day when Yeat kicked him on 30 September and he retaliated through his alt's rank — the one act the record can't soften, and the one he was restored from within a day once Divinestorm untangled the accusations. His summary of guild philosophy outlived all of it: "the mentality we set in Ninjas was always entertainment before some purple pixels."

supplier.name: Supplier
supplier.html:
Supplier earned his name. Across three years and nearly a thousand messages with Artimis, he was the guild's consumables economy in human form — flasks, protection potions, world-buff logistics, the LBRS venom-sack supply chain that made Viscidus killable. If a raid had what it needed, odds are Supplier had something to do with it.

He was Norwegian, precise, and allergic to sloppy thinking: the officer who asked what a poll was actually for before letting anyone run it, who told his fellow priests exactly how their channel would be run ("take it up with me directly"), and who de-escalated the guild's worst arguments by explaining what an expression meant in context. He was named Healing Officer at the September 2020 meeting and stayed in that seat through the December merge.

Two footnotes belong to him. It was his dry one-liner — "Shosanna was the only priest that got an item yesterday, fyi" — that became the last straw in Orish's dramatic exit, a fact he handled with characteristic equanimity ("Allright, nice to meet ya"). And in May 2021 he posted the "Dusk list": a set of tribute video links, one per guildmate — the closest thing the guild ever made to its own memorial before this site.

thepaladin.name: Thepaladin
thepaladin.html:
Thepaladin — Durm on Discord — was Sleep's paladin class leader for six weeks in the spring of 2020, and his 232-message thread with Artimis is one of the archive's richest seams. He was rich (the guild leader once asked, half in awe, where all the money came from), an alchemist, and the owner of the only Sulfuron Hammer in the guild, which put him first in line for the Eye of Sulfuras. Then Panadin got a hammer too, the rule became "everyone with the hammer rolls," and Durm's protest — sixty-two elites killed for one Eye — is the purest specimen of the guild's endless argument between earned priority and equal chance.

He got the class-leader job on 5 March ("It's your job now :p"), spent it designing debuff priorities and Lok'amir queues, and lost everything to a hacker in mid-April: someone logged into his account, the tickets went nowhere, and he never raided again. His last messages with Artimis are about bank fraud, not bosses. Chris covered the class as temporary leader, and the Eye he argued for outlived him as guild doctrine. His raid log ends on 8 April 2020, mid-era, mid-story — the archive's cleanest example of how Classic careers actually ended: not in drama, but in a support queue.

tsakimo.name: Tsakimo
tsakimo.html:
Tsakimo — Giorgos on Discord — ran the Wednesday rogues through the Dusk era, working the queue with Antzi across the two teams. His class-leader philosophy was transactional in the best sense: "loot is the reward — you make the effort, you focus, you pay for consumables, then you get loot." He handled the Nayla telephone-game with more patience than it deserved ("I will not take part in the insanity") and got a taste of the job's real burden when a relayed conversation turned out to have two versions: "now you can feel how it's working," Luivi told him, and he laughed.

He was blunt about standards — sign up by Friday or lose your spot, "no exceptions" — and blunt about himself, always discounting his own parses before anyone else could. The rogues under him stayed drama-free, which was the only metric he cared about.

ulfhild.name: Ulfhild
ulfhild.html:
Ulfhild was the guild's best hunter and made no apology for what that took: world buffs, full consumables, and total focus, every raid, for a character whose job was the damage meter. The Thursday team built its expectations around him, and he delivered so consistently that his one famous lapse became a governance crisis: on 17 September 2020, when a botched pull at the Ahn'Qiraj entrance wasted the buffs he'd spent hours collecting, he quit the raid on the spot.

The three-day officer argument that followed used his name as shorthand for a whole worldview. His defenders — and they were loud — pointed out that a near-perfect raider had been failed by the raid, not the other way around; his critics said no one player's buffs outweigh thirty-nine people's evening. He apologized in private, was back the next week, and kept doing what he always did: pulling, as one officer put it, more than his share. If everyone had pumped like Ulfhild, the mage leader mused that autumn, AQ would take forty-five minutes.

yeat.name: Yeat
yeat.html:
Yeat was the Thursday team's raid leader and master looter — the warrior who actually ran the nights, kept the loot in his bags between raids (occasionally to the guild banker's despair), and dialed in from work trips with lines like "please make preparations as if I'm not there." His raid-leading philosophy hardened after the September pull crisis: stricter comms, less fun on the mic, "I don't want that in my raid, full stop."

His name is attached to the era's strangest day. On 30 September 2020 he kicked Jón Snjór from the guild without consulting anyone — entangled in an accusation Divinestorm privately doubted — and the retaliation and protest quits that followed nearly cracked the guild. The reform that came out of it restricted kick powers for good. Yet the same record shows why he held the job: steady on loot fairness, first to volunteer for unglamorous logistics, and holder of the in-game guild-master character during the transition — which is how a mid-conflict kick became constitutionally possible in the first place.

zados.name: Zados
zados.html:
Zados was the guild's other half of the hunter brain trust and its co-leader in everything but title. From late 2019 onward he shows up wherever decisions were made: running the hunter class and its loot queues, keeping the debuff-slot priority list current, arguing rules in the officer chat with a debater's stamina, and organising the three-week hunter rotation that he, Artimis and Nereb shared when spots got scarce. His pet did enough damage to become a running joke in feral-druid comparisons.

The Dusk era slowly squeezed the old Sleep leadership out of power, and Zados felt it first. In the September 2020 server reshuffle his admin rights were flagged for removal, and when Divinestorm deleted a channel he liked, his reply — that he supposed he wasn't an officer any more, so whatever — is the driest line in the whole archive. He kept working anyway: the debuff documentation, hunter loot calls, and the long Discord-ping culture war he fought on pure principle ("I'm completely basing my reasoning on logic").

In December he was in the room for everything: skeptical of the new partners ("I have a pretty bad impression of ascension players so far"), blunt about roster choices, and finally the one who answered "when are we leaving and merging?" with "today would be good." He was in the first Four Horsemen kill and the Kel'Thuzad clear — one of the few who was there from the first Molten Core to the last boss of Classic.

nittedal.name: Ragie
nittedal.who: Tank leader across all three guilds; Pnats's brother; the main-tank half of the guild's longest loot argument.
